title: National Airlines 2511
summary: National Airlines Flight 2511, a Douglas DC-6, exploded in midair on January 6, 1960 while en route from New York to Miami. A dynamite explosion in the passenger cabin at approximately 2:33 a.m. significantly damaged the structural integrity of the aircraft and forced it into a wide right-hand turn. The aircraft suffered an in-flight disintegration at 2:38 a.m. near Unionville, North Carolina. The Civil Aeronautics Board concluded the plane was brought down by a bomb made of dynamite. All 34 crew and passengers perished.
probable_cause: The aircraft was brought down by a dynamite explosion in the passenger cabin located beneath the extreme right seat of seat row No. 7.

title: Scandinavian Airlines System 871
summary: A Scandinavian Airlines System Sud Aviation Caravelle crashed on approach to Ankara's Esenboğa International Airport on January 19, 1960. The aircraft was descending from FL135 to FL120 when it struck terrain at 3500 feet elevation between the Ankara range and the airport, 6 nm from the destination airport. All 42 occupants were killed. This was the first fatal crash of a Caravelle.
probable_cause: Unintentional descent below the authorized minimum flight altitude during final descent approach, though the reason for this descent could not be ascertained due to lack of conclusive evidence.

title: Avianca 671
summary: Avianca Flight 671, a Lockheed Constellation, made a heavy touchdown with a sinking speed exceeding 1200 feet per minute at Montego Bay on 21 January 1960. The aircraft bounced, skidded down the runway in flames, and came to rest upside down with its left wing broken off. Crew fatigue and inadequate training contributed to the excessive descent rate during landing, resulting in 37 fatalities.
probable_cause: Heavy landing with sinking speed well beyond the design maximum of 10 feet per second; contributing factors included crew fatigue and deficiencies in training leading to lapses in judgment.

factors.evidence: The aircraft made a heavy touchdown, bounced, and landed back on the runway with a sinking speed greater than the safe limit of 10 feet per second.
The rate of descent would have needed to be more than 1200 feet per minute to account for the aircraft's position and energy state on approach.
Crew fatigue was mentioned as a possible contributing factor to the excessive descent rate.
The ICAO report noted deficiencies in training that might have led to lapses in judgment affecting the crew's descent management.
The aircraft's left wing broke off, spilling aviation fuel and leading to a fire whose intensity kept firefighters from reaching the fuselage for about 20 minutes.

title: Aeroflot 315 (1960)
summary: Aeroflot Flight 315 was on final approach to Lviv on February 26, 1960, in icing conditions with cloud base at 150-200 meters. The Antonov An-10 descended normally until 95 meters altitude when flaps were set to 45 degrees and the aircraft rapidly pitched down. Investigation revealed that icing of the horizontal stabilizer created a supercritical angle of attack, causing sudden pitch-down when flaps were lowered to maximum setting. The aircraft impacted ground 1,400 meters short of runway with 20-25 degree pitch-down attitude. One passenger survived.
probable_cause: Icing of the horizontal stabilizer created a supercritical angle of attack that caused sudden pitch down when flaps were lowered to maximum 45 degree setting during final approach in icing conditions.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 710
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 710, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to Miami, broke up in midair over southern Indiana on March 17, 1960, after unexpectedly encountering clear-air turbulence at 18,000 ft; the right wing and part of the left wing separated and the aircraft plunged into farmland near Cannelton at over 600 mph, killing all 63 aboard. Investigators found the breakup closely resembled the 1959 Braniff Electra crash near Buffalo, Texas, and traced the cause to 'whirl mode' wing flutter: when an Electra's outboard engine mounting structure was damaged, high speed or turbulence could destroy the wing. The FAA restricted Electra operations and ordered Lockheed to redesign the structure.
probable_cause: The investigation attributed the in-flight breakup to whirl mode wing flutter: damage to an outboard engine's mounting structure, combined with high speed or turbulence, produced a destructive flutter that failed the wing -- the same unresolved defect implicated in the earlier Braniff Electra crash.

factors.evidence: The in-flight breakup of the Electra closely resembled the September 1959 crash of Braniff International Airways Flight 542 ... Investigators were unable to determine the cause at the time

when an Electra with damage to the mounting structures of one of its outboard engines operated at high speeds or in turbulence, a destructive phenomenon called whirl mode wing flutter could occur, leading to wing failure
the aircraft's right wing and part of the left wing separated, causing the fuselage to plummet and impact the ground

events.text: Flight 710 took off from Chicago Midway Airport at 2:38 p.m. with 57 passengers and a crew of 6.
At 3:13 p.m., passing the Scotland, Indiana waypoint at 18,000 ft, the crew reported to Indianapolis ARTC that the flight was proceeding normally.
Around the same time, U.S. Air Force B-57s operating nearby reported moderate to severe clear-air turbulence at high altitude, with one descending from 20,000-25,000 ft to 15,000 ft to escape it.

At about 3:20 p.m., in level flight at 400 mph, the aircraft's right wing separated from the fuselage, followed over six to ten seconds by the rest of the right wing and its engines; the outer left wing and its engine also broke away.

With its wings gone, the aircraft's momentum carried it more than 3 mi before it arced toward the ground, with an engine on the remaining left wing continuing to run at full power and accelerating the dive.
The aircraft struck farmland about 8 mi east of Cannelton, Indiana, nose-first at over 600 mph, leaving a crater about 15 ft deep and 30 ft wide.

title: Trans Australia Airlines 538
summary: On June 10, 1960, Trans Australia Airlines Flight 538, a Fokker Friendship, was making a nighttime approach to Mackay through fog and cloud cover when it descended below safe altitude and flew into the sea, killing all 29 occupants. The investigation could not determine a definitive cause but suggested possibilities including altimeter malfunction, misreading of the altimeter, or visual illusion over water at night deceiving the crew about altitude.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain during a nighttime approach in fog and cloud; cause not definitively established but altimeter malfunction or misreading, or visual illusion assessing height over water were considered.

title: Aeroflot 36 (1960)

location.name: 41 km north of Kyiv International Airport

summary: At cruising altitude near Kyiv checkpoint, the crew reported engine number four feathered and requested emergency landing. At 15:57 the crew reported number four engine and right wing on fire. The aircraft lost both engines number one and four when their support structures burned and failed, and both fuel tanks in the right wing ruptured, causing catastrophic structural damage. The aircraft crashed 41 km north of Kyiv International Airport with no survivors.
probable_cause: The number seven fuel injector of engine number four began leaking fuel into the engine housing, which eventually ignited after contact with high-temperature components. A contributing factor was the lack of engine fire extinguishing systems.

title: World Airways 830
summary: A Douglas DC-6 carrying American service members and dependents crashed into Mount Barrigada on Guam 50 seconds after takeoff on 19 September 1960, killing 80 of 94 occupants. The captain failed to adhere to standard departure procedures by making a right turn before the aircraft had climbed to the required 1,000 feet. The aircraft collided with the mountain during the climbing procedure, and most of the casualties were caused by a fire that broke out shortly before the aircraft came to a stop.
probable_cause: The pilot's failure to adhere to standard departure procedures by making a right turn before the aircraft had climbed to 1,000 feet, resulting in controlled flight into terrain.

title: Austrian Airlines flight 901
summary: During approach to Sheremetyevo, the crew's altimeters were set to conflicting pressure references. The captain's altimeter was adjusted to show zero feet at ground level, while the copilot's showed airport elevation, causing the crew to misjudge altitude. The aircraft struck trees 11 km short of the runway.
probable_cause: Altimeter setting discrepancy between captain and copilot that led the crew to misjudge the aircraft's height during approach.

title: Cal Poly football team plane crash
summary: A Curtiss C-46 carrying the Cal Poly Mustangs football team crashed shortly after takeoff from Toledo, Ohio in deteriorating visibility. The aircraft was overweight by 2,000 lb and the left engine lost partial power during the takeoff roll. The CAB determined loss of control during premature lift-off, with contributing factors including overweight condition, poor weather, and engine power loss.
probable_cause: Loss of control during a premature lift-off. Contributing factors were the overweight aircraft, weather conditions, and partial loss of power in the left engine.

title: 1960 New York air disaster
summary: On December 16, 1960, United Air Lines Flight 826, a Douglas DC-8 heading for Idlewild Airport, collided in midair with Trans World Airlines Flight 266, a Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation descending toward LaGuardia Airport. The Constellation crashed on Miller Field in Staten Island and the DC-8 in Park Slope, Brooklyn, killing all 128 aboard the two aircraft and six people on the ground. The accident was the world's deadliest aviation disaster at the time and remains the deadliest accident in United Airlines history.
probable_cause: United 826 had only one operational VOR receiver after the other became inoperative, which presented difficulty for the pilots to identify the PRESTON intersection. ATC was not informed of the inoperative receiver. The aircraft was estimated to be traveling at 301 knots when it collided, several miles beyond the PRESTON clearance limit.

title: 1960 Munich Convair 340 crash
summary: Shortly after takeoff from Munich-Riem in fog, the aircraft lost power to one of its two engines. Unable to maintain altitude with one engine and with visibility restricted by fog, the aircraft struck the 318 ft steeple of St. Paul's Church and subsequently crashed into a crowded Munich tramway car, killing 20 on the aircraft and 32 people on the ground.
probable_cause: Water in the fuel tank booster pump froze and blocked fuel inlets, depriving the engine of fuel and causing engine shutdown. The restricted visibility from fog prevented the crew from maintaining safe altitude and avoiding terrain.

factors.evidence: A crash investigation revealed water in the fuel tank booster pump; because water is more dense than fuel it can settle to the bottom of the tank and when it freezes it blocks inlets and deprives the engine of fuel.
This deprivation of fuel caused the Munich C-131 to lose power and eventually shut down the engine.
With bad visibility due to fog, unable to maintain altitude and with restricted visual references.
It hit the 318 ft steeple of St. Paul's Church and subsequently crashed into a crowded two-section Munich tramway car on Martin-Greif-Straße.

events.text: On 17 December 1960, the Samaritan was due to fly from Munich-Riem airport in Germany to RAF Northolt in the United Kingdom with 13 passengers and 7 crew.
Shortly after takeoff, the aircraft lost power to one of its two Pratt & Whitney R-2800 radial engines.
Unable to maintain altitude and with bad visibility due to fog, it hit the 318 ft steeple of St. Paul's Church next to the Oktoberfest site in the Ludwigsvorstadt borough.

Subsequently, at 2:10 PM, it crashed into a crowded two-section Munich tramway car on Martin-Greif-Straße, close to Bayerstraße, killing all 13 passengers and 7 crew members on the plane and 32 people on the ground.
